learn.hook: Why does a heavy almirah refuse to move until three people push together, and why does a rocket fly up by throwing gases down? Three laws explain it all!
points: A force is a push or a pull. Balanced forces cancel out and do not change motion; an unbalanced (net) force changes the speed or direction of motion.
First law: an object stays at rest, or keeps moving with uniform velocity in a straight line, unless an unbalanced force acts on it.
Second law: the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force. This gives F = m × a.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N). 1 N is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they do not cancel each other.

example.q: Think it through: What force is needed to give a 1000 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
steps: Use the second law: F = m × a.
m = 1000 kg, a = 2 m/s².

learn.reallife: ISRO's rockets push hot gases downwards at great speed, and by the third law the gases push the rocket upwards.

games.title: Match the law or term

quiz.q: A force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg trolley. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
steps: F = m × a
a = 5 m/s²
Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Multiplies force and mass instead of dividing

quiz.q: What force, in newtons, is needed to give a 1000 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
steps: F = m × a
Answer: 2000
quiz.mistake: Divides mass by acceleration or adds them

quiz.q: Which statement is Newton's first law of motion?
options: An object stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
All objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum
quiz.explain: The first law describes inertia: objects keep their state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts.
steps: First law: objects keep their state of rest or uniform straight-line motion
…unless an unbalanced force acts on them (inertia).
F = m × a is the second law; action–reaction is the third.
Answer: An object stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of Newton's three laws

quiz.q: You push a wall with a force of 50 N. What does the wall do?
quiz.explain: By the third law, the wall exerts an equal and opposite force of 50 N on your hands.
steps: Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
Action: you push the wall with 50 N.
Reaction: the wall pushes you back with 50 N.
Answer: Pushes you back with 50 N
quiz.mistake: Thinks objects that do not move cannot exert a force

quiz.q: Action and reaction forces are equal and opposite. Why don't they cancel each other?
options: One of them is always bigger
They act in the same direction
quiz.explain: Forces cancel only when they act on the same body. Action acts on one body and reaction on the other.
steps: Forces cancel only when they act on the same body.
Action acts on one body, reaction on the other.
Answer: They act on different bodies
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal and opposite forces always cancel, wherever they act

quiz.q: How does a rocket move upwards?
options: It pushes against the air above it
Hot gases pushed down by the rocket push the rocket up
quiz.explain: This is the third law: the rocket pushes gases down (action) and the gases push the rocket up (reaction). It works even in space with no air.
steps: Third law: the rocket pushes hot gases downwards (action).
The gases push the rocket upwards (reaction).
It needs no air to push against.
Answer: Hot gases pushed down by the rocket push the rocket up
quiz.mistake: Thinks a rocket needs air to push against

quiz.q: In a tug of war, both teams pull the rope with 500 N in opposite directions. What happens?
options: The rope does not move, because the forces are balanced
The rope moves towards the second team
The rope moves towards the first team
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite forces on the same rope are balanced, so the net force is zero and the rope stays still.
steps: Forces on the rope: 500 N one way, 500 N the other.
Net force = 500 − 500 = 0 N, so the forces are balanced.
Balanced forces do not change motion.
Answer: The rope does not move, because the forces are balanced
quiz.mistake: Thinks there is always a winner when forces act

quiz.q: What is 1 newton?
options: The weight of 1 kg on the Earth
The work done in moving 1 m
The force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
quiz.explain: From F = m × a, 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s². The weight of 1 kg on the Earth is about 9.8 N.
steps: F = m × a.
1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s².
The weight of 1 kg on Earth is about 9.8 N, not 1 N.
Answer: The force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
quiz.mistake: Confuses 1 newton with the weight of 1 kg

teach.ask: Gappu pushes a pebble with his beak: "When I push the pebble, does the pebble push me too? And why does it speed up?"
teach.praise: Chirp! The pebble stays still until a net force acts (first law), it speeds up depending on force and mass (F = ma), and it pushes back on me equally (third law)!
teach.nudge: You explained why it moves, but does the pebble push back on my beak too? Which law says that?

revise.summary: A force is a push or pull; only an unbalanced force changes motion. Newton's first law describes inertia, the second gives F = m × a, and the third says action and reaction are equal, opposite and act on different bodies.
focus: Using F = m × a; the newton
Why action and reaction don't cancel; rockets
remember: F = m × a; 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s²
First law: rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts
Third law: equal and opposite; on different bodies
traps: Action–reaction forces never cancel; they act on different bodies
1 N is not the weight of 1 kg (that is about 9.8 N)
Rockets don't need air to push against

learn.hook: Why do you lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly, and why does a fielder pull back his hands while catching a hard cricket ball?
points: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion.
Mass is the measure of inertia. A loaded truck has much more inertia than a bicycle, so it is harder to start or stop.
Momentum p = mass × velocity. It is a vector, and its SI unit is kg m/s. A parked car has zero momentum.
A force changes momentum. Taking more time to stop a moving object means a smaller force is needed. That is why a fielder pulls his hands back.
Law of conservation of momentum: when no external force acts, the total momentum of a system stays the same. A gun recoils backwards when a bullet is fired forwards.

example.q: Think it through: A 0.02 kg bullet is fired from a 2 kg gun at 100 m/s. With what speed does the gun recoil?
steps: Before firing, everything is at rest, so total momentum = 0.
Momentum of the bullet = 0.02 × 100 = 2 kg m/s forwards.
The gun must have 2 kg m/s backwards so the total stays 0.
Recoil speed = 2 ÷ 2 = 1 m/s.

learn.reallife: Seat belts, airbags and the sand pit in a long-jump event all increase the time taken to stop, which reduces the force on the body.

games.title: Inertia and momentum: true or false?
items: A heavier object has more inertia than a lighter one
Mass is the measure of inertia.
A parked car has a large momentum because it is heavy
Its velocity is zero, so its momentum (m × v) is zero.
Passengers fall forward when a bus suddenly stops because of the inertia of motion
Their bodies tend to keep moving forward when the bus stops.
Momentum has no direction
Momentum is a vector; it has the same direction as the velocity.
When a gun fires a bullet, the gun moves backwards
Total momentum is conserved, so the gun recoils opposite to the bullet.

items.q: Momentum of a parked 1000 kg car?
Momentum 100 kg m/s, mass 20 kg: velocity in m/s?

quiz.q: When a moving bus brakes suddenly, the standing passengers tend to fall forward. Why?
options: The air in the bus pushes them
Their bodies tend to keep moving forward due to inertia
quiz.explain: The bus stops, but the passengers' bodies tend to continue in motion because of inertia, so they lurch forward.
steps: Inertia: an object resists change in its state of motion.
The bus stops, but the passengers' bodies tend to keep moving forward.
Answer: Their bodies tend to keep moving forward due to inertia
quiz.mistake: Thinks a forward force acts on the passengers

quiz.q: A coin is placed on a card over a glass. The card is flicked away quickly and the coin drops into the glass. This shows
quiz.explain: The card moves away so fast that the coin, at rest, tends to stay at rest and then falls into the glass.
steps: The coin is at rest on the card.
The card is pulled away quickly; the coin tends to stay at rest.
It then falls into the glass.
Answer: inertia of rest
quiz.mistake: Thinks the coin should move along with the card

quiz.q: Which quantity is a measure of the inertia of an object?
quiz.explain: The greater the mass, the greater the inertia, and the harder it is to change the object's motion.
steps: Mass is the measure of inertia.
More mass → harder to start or stop.
Answer: Its mass
quiz.mistake: Confuses mass with size (volume)

quiz.q: A 50 kg girl runs at 4 m/s. What is her momentum in kg m/s?
steps: p = m × v
= 200 kg m/s
Answer: 200
quiz.mistake: Divides or adds mass and velocity instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Why does a fielder pull his hands backwards while catching a fast cricket ball?
options: To throw the ball back quickly
To increase the time of stopping the ball, so less force acts on his hands
quiz.explain: The ball's momentum must become zero. Spreading this change over a longer time needs a smaller force, so it hurts less.
steps: The ball's momentum must be brought to zero.
Pulling the hands back increases the stopping time.
More time → smaller force needed on the hands.
Answer: To increase the time of stopping the ball, so less force acts on his hands
quiz.mistake: Does not link a longer stopping time with a smaller force

quiz.q: A gun recoils when a bullet is fired. Which law explains this?
quiz.explain: Total momentum before firing is zero, so after firing the forward momentum of the bullet equals the backward momentum of the gun.
steps: Before firing, total momentum = 0.
After firing: bullet forward momentum = gun backward momentum.
This is conservation of momentum.
Answer: Conservation of momentum
quiz.mistake: Does not apply momentum conservation to firing

quiz.q: A 0.02 kg bullet leaves a 2 kg gun at 100 m/s. What is the recoil speed of the gun in m/s?
quiz.explain: Bullet momentum = 0.02 × 100 = 2 kg m/s. The gun gets 2 kg m/s backwards, so its speed = 2 ÷ 2 = 1 m/s.
steps: Bullet: 0.02 × 100 = 2 kg m/s
Gun: 2 kg × v = 2 kg m/s
v = 1 m/s
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks the gun moves at the same speed as the bullet

quiz.q: Which has the greatest inertia?
quiz.explain: The loaded truck has by far the greatest mass, so it has the greatest inertia.
steps: Mass is the measure of inertia.
A loaded truck has by far the greatest mass.
Answer: A loaded truck
quiz.mistake: Thinks inertia depends on speed instead of mass

teach.ask: Gappu tumbles forward when the branch he sits on stops swaying: "Who pushed me? Nobody was there!"
teach.praise: Tweet! Nobody pushed me: my body just kept moving because of inertia, and more mass means more inertia. Momentum is mass times velocity!
teach.nudge: My body was moving with the branch. When the branch stopped, what did my body want to keep doing?

revise.summary: Inertia is resistance to change in motion, and mass measures it. Momentum p = m × v; a force changes momentum, and with no external force total momentum is conserved, as in gun recoil.
focus: Mass as the measure of inertia
Increasing stopping time to reduce force; conservation of momentum
remember: p = m × v; SI unit kg m/s
No external force → total momentum constant (gun recoil)
traps: A heavier object has more inertia, not less
A parked car has zero momentum
Fielders pull hands back to reduce force, not to increase momentum

learn.hook: The same force that makes a mango drop from a tree keeps the Moon going round the Earth. Isaac Newton realised it is all one force: gravitation!
points: Universal law of gravitation: every object attracts every other object with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G m₁m₂ ÷ d².
G is the universal gravitational constant, about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². Because G is so small, the pull between everyday objects is too weak to notice.
Near the Earth's surface, all freely falling objects have the same acceleration due to gravity, g ≈ 9.8 m/s², if air resistance is ignored. g is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator.
Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the force with which a planet pulls an object: W = m × g, measured in newtons.
On the Moon, g is about one-sixth of its value on the Earth, so you would weigh about one-sixth as much there. The Moon's pull is the main cause of tides.

example.q: Think it through: Vikram's mass is 60 kg. What is his weight on the Earth, and what would his mass be on the Moon? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
steps: Weight on the Earth = m × g = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N.
Mass is the amount of matter in his body.
Going to the Moon does not change the amount of matter.
So his mass on the Moon is still 60 kg (but his weight would be about one-sixth of 588 N, about 98 N).
example.answer: Weight on the Earth = 588 N; mass on the Moon = 60 kg.

learn.reallife: Chandrayaan-3's lander had to be guided down carefully to the Moon, whose gravity is much weaker than the Earth's, and fishermen along the coast plan their trips around tides caused by the Moon.

games.title: Mass or weight?
items: Measured in kilograms
Same on the Earth and the Moon
Amount of matter in a body
Measure of inertia
Measured in newtons
Less on the Moon than on the Earth
Force with which a planet pulls a body
Equal to m × g

games.title: Gravitation: true or false?
items: The Earth attracts the Moon, and the Moon also attracts the Earth
Gravitation acts between every pair of objects, and the forces are equal and opposite.
Gravitational force acts only between very large objects like planets
It acts between all objects, but between small objects it is too weak to notice.
If the distance between two objects is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes half
The force depends on 1/d², so doubling d makes the force one-fourth.
The value of g is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator
The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, so the poles are a little closer to its centre.
An astronaut's mass becomes zero in space
Mass is the amount of matter and does not change; only the weight changes.

quiz.q: Who gave the universal law of gravitation?
quiz.explain: Isaac Newton stated the universal law of gravitation in the 17th century.
steps: The universal law of gravitation: F = G m₁m₂ ÷ d².
It was given by Isaac Newton.
Answer: Isaac Newton
quiz.mistake: Confuses Newton with Galileo, who studied falling bodies

quiz.q: If the distance between two objects is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes
quiz.explain: Force is inversely proportional to d². Doubling d makes d² four times bigger, so the force becomes one-fourth.
steps: F ∝ 1 ÷ d².
d → 2d makes d² → 4d².
Answer: one-fourth
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the distance is squared in the law

quiz.q: A boy has a mass of 60 kg on the Earth. What is his mass on the Moon?
quiz.explain: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change from place to place. Only weight changes.
steps: Mass is the amount of matter; it is the same everywhere.
Only weight (W = m × g) changes on the Moon.
Mass on the Moon = 60 kg.
Answer: 60 kg
quiz.mistake: Confuses mass with weight, which is about one-sixth on the Moon

quiz.q: What is the weight, in newtons, of a 60 kg boy on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
steps: W = m × g
Answer: 588
quiz.mistake: Gives the mass in kg as the weight, or divides by g

quiz.q: What is the approximate value of g near the Earth's surface, in m/s²?
quiz.explain: The acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface is about 9.8 m/s². About 1.6 m/s² is the Moon's value.
steps: Near Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.8 m/s².
6.67 is part of G; about 1.6 m/s² is the Moon's g.
Answer: 9.8
quiz.mistake: Confuses g with the constant G or with the Moon's value

quiz.q: In a tube with all the air removed, a feather and a coin are dropped together. What happens?
options: The feather floats and never lands
quiz.explain: Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration g, whatever their mass.
steps: In a vacuum there is no air resistance.
All freely falling objects then have the same acceleration g.
So feather and coin fall together.
Answer: They land together
quiz.mistake: Thinks heavier objects always fall faster

quiz.q: A stone weighs 60 N on the Earth. About how much will it weigh on the Moon, in newtons?
quiz.explain: The Moon's g is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so the weight becomes about 60 ÷ 6 = 10 N.
steps: Weight on the Moon ≈ weight on the Earth ÷ 6
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Thinks weight stays the same everywhere, like mass

quiz.q: What is the main cause of ocean tides on the Earth?
options: The gravitational pull of the Moon
quiz.explain: The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth's oceans, making the water rise and fall twice a day at most places.
steps: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans.
This makes the sea rise and fall.
Answer: The gravitational pull of the Moon
quiz.mistake: Links tides with winds or waves instead of gravitation

teach.ask: Gappu wants to be an astronaut: "If I fly to the Moon, will I become lighter? Will there be less of me?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! My mass stays the same everywhere, but my weight, the Moon's pull on me, would be about one-sixth. Less of a pull, not less of me!
teach.nudge: Does the amount of me change on the Moon, or only how hard I am pulled down?

revise.summary: Every object attracts every other: F = G m₁m₂ ÷ d². Near Earth all objects fall with g ≈ 9.8 m/s²; mass stays the same everywhere while weight W = m × g changes, being about one-sixth on the Moon.
focus: Universal law of gravitation and the inverse-square rule
Value and meaning of G and g
Mass vs weight; W = m × g
Free fall in a vacuum; Moon's gravity and tides
remember: F = G m₁m₂ ÷ d²; G ≈ 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg²
W = m × g (newtons); mass unchanged everywhere
traps: Doubling distance makes force one-fourth, not half
Mass does not change on the Moon; weight does
Without air, a feather and a coin fall together
